chunks: "A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one chip: CPU, flash for the program, SRAM, and the peripherals you need to talk to the world, like GPIO, timers, ADC, UART, SPI and I2C.
You power it, give it a clock, and it runs. A microprocessor is mostly the CPU.
It needs external DRAM, storage like flash or eMMC, a power-management chip and often external peripherals, though modern application processors integrate many interfaces.
That integration difference drives everything else.
MCUs are cheap, low power, simple to design with a two-layer board, boot in milliseconds, and are deterministic: a hardware interrupt responds in tens to hundreds of nanoseconds.
They run bare-metal or an RTOS.

MPUs are faster, with caches, an MMU and gigahertz clocks, so they can run Linux with networking, a GUI, cameras and machine learning, but they cost more, draw watts, need DDR routing and four-plus layers, boot in seconds, and have non-deterministic timing.
So for a thermostat, a motor controller or a battery sensor I'd pick an MCU; for a router, a camera or an HMI with a rich display I'd pick an MPU.
Often a product uses both: an MPU for the application and an MCU for real-time control.
And the line is blurring: Cortex-M7 MCUs run at 600 megahertz, and SoCs combine Cortex-A cores with a Cortex-M real-time core."
